matter_reference_date_basis: matter_reference_date field of candidates/matters/M017.json (exam session OCTOBER 2025). The lease itself is said to commence in 2020, so the law is taken as at the October 2025 sitting while the instrument is dated 2020; where the two diverge it is noted in temporal_note.
corpus_gaps: No stamp duty rate is in the corpus. Section 3(1) of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 fixes the rate by Ministerial Order published in the Gazette, and no such Order (and no rate schedule for leases) has been extracted. The calculation asked for in M017-Q01 cannot be completed from statute text alone.
The Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 as extracted carries no Schedule of rates (a grep for 'Schedule' over 43-1982 returns no match), so the older regime supplies no fallback rate either.
No Ministerial Order under section 5 of Act No. 12 of 2006 (exemptions) is in the corpus, so it cannot be confirmed whether a residential lease of this kind is exempt.

The corpus has no general statute on the content of lease covenants. The reciprocal rights and duties of lessor and lessee in Sri Lanka rest on Roman-Dutch common law and on conveyancing practice, neither of which is reachable through this tool.
No authority in the corpus governs the appropriation of an advance payment against future rental instalments; that turns on the terms of the parties' agreement and on the general law of obligations.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: there shall be charged a duty (hereinafter to be called "stamp duty") at such rate as the Minister may determine by Order published in the Gazette on every "specified instrument"- (a) executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka
provisions.why_relevant: The charging provision for stamp duty on the lease agreement, an instrument to be executed in Sri Lanka. It is also the provision that shows why the amount cannot be computed from the Act: the rate is not in the Act, it is set by Ministerial Order in the Gazette.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2006 with no amendment events recorded on this section, so the same text applies at the stated 2020 execution and at the October 2025 reference date.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: (h) a promissory note; (i) a lease or hire of any property; (j) a receipt or discharge given for any money or other property;
provisions.why_relevant: Defines "specified instrument" for the purposes of section 3 and brings a lease of any property within the charge. Without it the lease between Mala and Sheela is not shown to be chargeable at all.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2006, no amendment events recorded on this section.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: in cases where there is an agreement to the contrary, stamp duty shall be payable:- (a) in the case of a policy of insurance, by the person effecting the insurance; (b) in the case of a transfer or assignment of any share, by the transferee or assignee of such share; (c) in the case of a lease, by the lessee;
provisions.why_relevant: Identifies Sheela, as lessee, as the person liable for the stamp duty on the lease, subject to any agreement to the contrary between the parties.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2006; amended in 2008 by Act No. 10 of 2008 s.2, which inserted paragraphs (dd) and (ddd). That amendment predates both the 2020 execution and the October 2025 reference date, and paragraph (c) on leases is unaffected by it.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Stamp duty payable on any specified instrument relating to a mortgage or lease of any immovable property may be paid, prior to, or at the time of, the execution of the specified instrument, to a prescribed bank.
provisions.why_relevant: Governs how and when the duty on a lease of immovable property is paid and evidenced. It bears on the practical answer to a 'stamp duty payable' question even though it does not supply the rate.
provisions.temporal_note: Substituted in 2008 by Act No. 10 of 2008 s.3; the substituted text is the one in force at both the 2020 execution and the October 2025 reference date.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: the provisions of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982, relating to the Imposition of Stamp Duty (other than any instrument relating to the transfer of immovable property, the transfer of motor vehicles or documents filed in Court), Exemptions and any other provision in the aforesaid Act, shall, in so far as the same are inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, have no operation
provisions.why_relevant: Settles which of the two stamp duty statutes in the corpus governs a lease executed after 2006: the imposition provisions of the 1982 Act give way to Act No. 12 of 2006, so the rate must be found in an Order under section 3 of the 2006 Act.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 2006, no amendment events recorded on this section.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
provisions.why_relevant: A lease of a house for two years is outside the one-month exclusion, so the agreement must be in writing and notarially executed and attested. This fixes the form of the instrument that will carry the covenants asked for in Q03, and the instrument on which stamp duty is charged.
provisions.temporal_note: Section 2 carries amendment events in 1947, 2022 and 2024. The 2022 and 2024 amendments concern the thumb impression and transfer deed requirements in subsections (1) and (2); the exclusion of leases at will or for not more than one month relied on here is long-standing. The 2020 execution predates the 2022 and 2024 amendments, so a verifier should confirm which text governs the instrument as against the October 2025 reference date.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: Stamp duty is a wholly statutory charge. Liability, the identity of the payer and the manner of payment all follow from the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 without any need for judicial authority or common law. The question is nevertheless not answerable on the corpus as frozen, because the operative rate lives in a Ministerial Order under section 3(1) that has not been extracted.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a two-year lease of a house in Colombo is a chargeable instrument for stamp duty purposes.
What consideration forms the base of the charge: whether the two years of rental, the refundable deposit of Rs. 300,000 and the advance of Rs. 600,000 all enter the computation.
What rate applies to a lease of immovable property, and by whom and when the duty must be paid.

questions.hop_count_basis: The charging provision s.3(1) plus the definition of "specified instrument" in s.4(i) that brings a lease within it. A third hop to the rate Order would be needed to reach a figure, but that Order is not in the corpus.

enrichment.original_background: Mala is living with her daughter in Kurunegala. She intends to lease out her own house in Colombo for a monthly rental of Rs. 100,000/ for two years to Sheela. The rentals of the house have to be paid on the 20th day of each month commencing from 2020. Mala obtained a refundable deposit of Rs. 300,000/ from Sheela. She also obtained an advance payment of Rs. 600,000/ and intends it to be set off against the 1st year's monthly rental.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether stamp duty is chargeable on the two-year lease of Mala's Colombo house to Sheela, on what base and at what rate, and who must pay it.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 s.3(1) charges stamp duty on every "specified instrument" executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka, at such rate as the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette. Section 4(i) makes "a lease or hire of any property" a specified instrument. Section 6(c) makes the duty on a lease payable by the lessee unless the parties agree otherwise. Section 8(2) allows the duty on a lease of immovable property to be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at the time of execution, with the bank's certificate affixed to the instrument. Section 13 makes the imposition provisions of the Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 inoperative so far as they are inconsistent with the 2006 Act, so the rate for a post-2006 lease must be found in an Order under s.3(1) of the 2006 Act and not in the 1982 Act.
gold_answer_draft.application: The lease between Mala and Sheela is an instrument to be executed in Sri Lanka in respect of a house in Colombo, and a lease of property falls squarely within Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.4(i), so duty is chargeable under s.3(1). Unless the agreement provides otherwise, s.6(c) puts the burden on Sheela as lessee, and s.8(2) allows payment to a prescribed bank at or before execution. The base for the charge would be the rental consideration secured by the lease, on these facts Rs. 100,000 a month for twenty-four months, that is Rs. 2,400,000. Two further points affect the base: the Rs. 600,000 advance is a prepayment of part of the first year's rental rather than an addition to it, and the Rs. 300,000 deposit is refundable and so arguably not consideration at all. Both the rate and the treatment of the deposit are matters for the Ministerial Order under s.3(1), and no such Order is in the frozen corpus. The Act supplies no percentage, no slab and no minimum, so no figure can be computed from the statutory text alone.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Stamp duty is chargeable on the lease agreement and is prima facie payable by Sheela as lessee, but the amount cannot be calculated from the corpus. The question is recorded as blocked for missing authority: the rate Order made under s.3(1) of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, and any exemption Order under s.5, are not part of the frozen corpus, and the answer must not be completed by quoting a rate from memory.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka at the rate the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette.
A lease or hire of any property is a specified instrument for the purposes of the charging section.
In the case of a lease the stamp duty is payable by the lessee, unless the parties have agreed to the contrary.
The duty on a lease of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at the time of execution of the instrument.

For a lease executed after 2006 the rate must be sought in an Order under section 3(1) of the 2006 Act, because the imposition provisions of the Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 have no operation so far as they are inconsistent with the 2006 Act.
The proposed lease of Mala's Colombo house to Sheela for two years is a lease of property and so a specified instrument on which duty is chargeable.
Absent a contrary term in the lease, Sheela as lessee bears the duty.

The rental consideration passing under the lease on the stated facts is Rs. 100,000 a month for twenty-four months, that is Rs. 2,400,000, the Rs. 600,000 advance being a prepayment of part of that sum rather than an addition to it.
No figure for the stamp duty can be produced, because the rate is fixed only by a Ministerial Order under section 3(1) and no such Order, and no exemption Order under section 5, is in the corpus.

The Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act No. 12 of 2006 imposes the charge but delegates the rate to a Ministerial Order published in the Gazette under s.3(1), and no such Order is in the frozen corpus; the Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 as extracted carries no Schedule of rates either. Whether the refundable deposit enters the base is likewise a matter for the Order. A number cannot be given without quoting a rate from outside the corpus.

legal_issues.issue: How the Rs. 600,000 advance is to be appropriated against the first year's monthly rentals, and what monthly sum Sheela must therefore pay during the first year.
Whether the refundable deposit of Rs. 300,000 affects the monthly rental payable, or is held separately and repayable at the end of the term.

questions.hop_count_basis: No statutory provision in the corpus is needed to answer the question; the calculation runs off the contractual terms alone, so there are no indispensable dependencies to count.

enrichment.original_background: Mala is living with her daughter in Kurunegala. She intends to lease out her own house in Colombo for a monthly rental of Rs. 100,000/ for two years to Sheela. The rentals of the house have to be paid on the 20th day of each month commencing from 2020. Mala obtained a refundable deposit of Rs. 300,000/ from Sheela. She also obtained an advance payment of Rs. 600,000/ and intends it to be set off against the 1st year's monthly rental.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What monthly sum Sheela has to pay as rental during the first year, given the Rs. 600,000 advance that Mala intends to set off against the first year's monthly rental.
gold_answer_draft.rule: No provision in the frozen statutory corpus fixes how an advance payment is to be appropriated against future rental instalments. The point is governed by the terms of the lease the parties execute and by the general law of obligations, which for a Sri Lankan lease is Roman-Dutch common law. The question is therefore reserved rather than answered as statute-based gold.
gold_answer_draft.application: On the stated intention the Rs. 600,000 advance is applied against the first year's rentals. Twelve months at Rs. 100,000 comes to Rs. 1,200,000; setting Rs. 600,000 against that leaves Rs. 600,000 to be found over the twelve months, that is Rs. 50,000 on the 20th of each month during the first year, with the full Rs. 100,000 falling due monthly in the second year. The refundable deposit of Rs. 300,000 is a separate security sum repayable at the end of the term and on these facts does not reduce the rental. This reading is not the only one open: the advance could instead be exhausted against the first six months in full, leaving nothing payable for six months and Rs. 100,000 a month thereafter. Which applies depends on how the covenant is drafted, and neither reading rests on any statutory provision.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: On the appropriation the facts most naturally support, Sheela pays Rs. 50,000 a month during the first year. The question is reserved: the answer turns on the construction of the parties' agreement and on the common law of lease, not on any statute in the corpus, and the set-off mechanism should be settled in the drafting rather than assumed.

answer_claims.claim_text: The corpus contains no statutory rule on the appropriation of an advance payment against future rental instalments; the point is contractual and governed by the general law of obligations.
The first year's rental at Rs. 100,000 a month totals Rs. 1,200,000, against which the Rs. 600,000 advance leaves Rs. 600,000 payable over twelve months, or Rs. 50,000 on the 20th of each month.
The Rs. 300,000 refundable deposit is a security sum repayable at the end of the term and does not reduce the monthly rental.

Sheela pays Rs. 50,000 a month during the first year on the even set-off reading, but an alternative appropriation exhausting the advance over the first six months is equally open on the facts as stated.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The form of the instrument is statutory: a lease of a house for two years falls outside the one-month exclusion in Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) and must be in writing and notarially executed. The content of the covenants themselves, payment of rent, use, repair, sub-letting, deposit, re-entry and quiet enjoyment, is not prescribed by any statute in the corpus. It rests on the Roman-Dutch common law of lease and on conveyancing practice, so a complete answer needs non-statutory authority.

legal_issues.issue: In what form the lease must be executed for a two-year lease of a house.
What covenants should be drafted to record the rent and its due date, the set-off of the advance, the refundable deposit, and the parties' obligations as to use, repair, sub-letting and re-entry.

questions.hop_count_basis: One statutory step, the notarial execution requirement in Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1), which fixes the form of the instrument. The covenants themselves add no statutory hop because no provision in the corpus prescribes them.

enrichment.original_background: Mala is living with her daughter in Kurunegala. She intends to lease out her own house in Colombo for a monthly rental of Rs. 100,000/ for two years to Sheela. The rentals of the house have to be paid on the 20th day of each month commencing from 2020. Mala obtained a refundable deposit of Rs. 300,000/ from Sheela. She also obtained an advance payment of Rs. 600,000/ and intends it to be set off against the 1st year's monthly rental.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What five covenants should be drafted into the lease between Mala as lessor and Sheela as lessee, and what statutory constraint governs the form of the instrument that carries them.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1) excludes only a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month from the requirement of a notarially executed writing, so a two-year lease of a house must be in writing, signed before a licensed notary public and the witnesses and attested by that notary, or it will not avail in law. Beyond that requirement of form, the corpus prescribes no content for lease covenants; the reciprocal duties of lessor and lessee come from the Roman-Dutch common law of lease and from conveyancing practice. Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.6(c) is relevant to one covenant only, in that it makes the duty payable by the lessee unless the lease agrees otherwise, so the parties may allocate it expressly.
gold_answer_draft.application: Working from the facts, the covenants that need drafting are: a covenant to pay rent of Rs. 100,000 per month on the 20th day of each month of the two-year term; a covenant recording the Rs. 600,000 advance and the manner in which it is set off against the first year's rental, so that the sum actually payable each month in year one is unambiguous; a covenant on the Rs. 300,000 refundable deposit, stating that it is held as security, is not to be treated as rent, and is repayable at the end of the term subject to deductions for arrears or damage; a covenant restricting Sheela to use of the premises as a private dwelling house and prohibiting sub-letting or assignment without Mala's written consent; and a covenant on maintenance and repair, allocating interior upkeep and utility charges to Sheela and structural repair to Mala, coupled with a right of re-entry on default in rent and a covenant for quiet enjoyment while the rent is paid. Because Mala is in Kurunegala and the house is in Colombo, a covenant on notices and on inspection upon reasonable notice is worth adding, as is an express covenant on who bears the stamp duty, since without one the duty falls on Sheela as lessee. Which five a marker expects, and the exact wording, is a drafting judgment shaped by practice rather than by statute.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The lease must be notarially executed because it exceeds one month, and the covenants above respond to the facts given. The question is reserved rather than proposed as statute-only gold: no provision in the corpus prescribes the content of lease covenants, so the model answer rests on the common law of lease and on conveyancing practice, which lie outside the frozen statutory corpus.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month must be in writing and notarially executed and attested, since only a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month is excluded.
Stamp duty on a lease falls on the lessee unless the lease provides to the contrary, so the parties may allocate it by an express covenant.
The two-year term of Mala's lease to Sheela puts it outside the one-month exclusion, so the instrument carrying the covenants must be a notarially executed lease.

The covenants the facts call for are payment of rent on the 20th of each month, set-off of the Rs. 600,000 advance against the first year, treatment and repayment of the Rs. 300,000 deposit, restriction on use and on sub-letting or assignment, and allocation of repair with a right of re-entry on default and quiet enjoyment while rent is paid.
The content of the covenants cannot be settled from the corpus, because no statute in it prescribes the terms of a lease; the drafting rests on the common law of lease and on conveyancing practice.
